channel.title: Attoparsec
channel.description: Technical art for curious people -- the Seattle-area kinetic sculpture/industrial art group Attoparsec.

videos.desc: UBC CS band Algorithm at the 2009 Coffeehouse
UBC CS band Algorithm at the 2009 Coffeehouse
UBC CS band Algorithm at the 2009 Coffeehouse
Prototype testing of the gear layout for my self-adjusting electro-mechanical sunglasses
First test of the entire suite of LASER MEDUSA HELMET modules, all mounted and wired into the central power system.
The LASER MEDUSA HELMET complete except for tilt sensors, mounted on the helmet and powered up.
A demo of the complete electro-mechanical sunglasses system, showing the variable opacity of the polarized sheets.
I was challenged to prove I could spin a pen around my thumb. SO BE IT!
A demo of the 5-panel metal Jacob's Ladder prototype using bike chain for the connecting straps.
Test run of the Jacob's Ladder device. Currently it cannot reliably trigger cascades, but otherwise it is definitely coming together.

This is the all-but finished Jacob's Ladder No. 1. It hasn't been converted to a wall mount yet, but otherwise it is functionally and aesthetically compete. New since the previous video: standoffs for the eventually wall mount, wood stain, brass label plates, slower motor speed and finished electronics packaging.
Higher quality demonstration video of the 2009 Electro-Mechanical Sunglasses. A flashlight is placed behind one of the lenses to show the changing opacity due to the rotating polarized sheets.
Test of the Jacob's Ladder No. 1installation at the Night Kitchen
Test run of the fireprop, a mechanical representation of fire made as a custom stage prop for a friend.
Prototype of a parallel motion for use in my Kalamazoo/handcar project

An old video of a test run of the GYRE freefall robot. Important thing to be watching for: it is spinning, then the air jets fire and it more or less stops. The robot was built as our project for the NASA Reduced Gravity Student Flight Opportunity Program, and flew in 2003 and 2006.

A demonstration of the pump motion on the Kalamazoo (hand car) that I'm building for Burning Man this year. The pump arm isn't currently connected to the drive train, but this gives a pretty good idea what it will look like when done. Project updates can be found on the Attoparsec blog: http://attoparsec-gadgets.blogspot.com/

videos.t: Kalamazoo: Mounting rungs, some brakes, horn
videos.desc: The second video update of the Kalamazoo construction. Brake levers and the brake cable sheath have been added, mounting rungs forged and bolted on, and an antique, foot-switch-activated car horn mounted.
Overview of the last week's worth of work adding better chain tensioning systems to the Kalamazoo.

We took the Kalamazoo out for its first road test today. The results were... not great. The steering system is going to have to be completely redesigned, and homemade fixie wheels are obviously not a good idea. But, it's still nice to see it out of the garage.

Showing off the new steering mechanism for the Kalamazoo. Kind of a rush job, but it looks like it will work okay. Turning radius is a joke, oh well. Will need to link it to the other caster with a tie rod, but that will be easy enough.
Quick overview of the offset steering lever, complete steering mechanism, and flywheel improvement.

Third road test of the Kalamazoo, testing the final steering system, the new 27" fixed gear wheels, and the prototype lantern mounting. Drive chains were not properly adjusted, however, hence the unpleasant motion at points.
Final road test of the Kalamazoo before Burning Man. It works! Mostly!

Quick test of the el-wire sequencer board I'm putting together. This is just one of the 8 channels the final version will have, etched on a scrap of copper clad as a test. Hopefully the resulting product will be seen at SeaCompression 2010.
Demonstration of the Difference Engine at the Computer Science Museum. This is as steampunk as it gets, folks.
Demonstration of the Difference Engine at the Computer Science Museum. This is as steampunk as it gets, folks.
Demonstration of the Difference Engine at the Computer Science Museum. This is as steampunk as it gets, folks.

A test of the el-wire jumpsuit I'm working on, showing the full range of 21 independently controlled strands, with PWM to create a nice fade in/fade out effect. The final version will use an accelerometer as input for the position of the light band.
What I see if I look down while wearing the lightsuit.
The latest Attoparsec invention: the lightsuit! 21 independently controllable el-wire strands mounted on a fetching and stylish military-style jumpsuit.
Got a new batch of business cards laser cut at Metrix, thought I'd grab a video of the process.
Quick demo of the Phoenix Hexapod I recently acquired for research for a future Attoparsec project.
Testing a cheap little stocking stuffer on Christmas morning 2010

Demonstration of the etched brass fan I made for a SteamCon II costume. It is made of 22 gage brass sheet, etched with ferric chloride and then aged with ammonia and salt water. More details on the construction here: http://attoparsec-gadgets.blogspot.com/2011/01/etched-brass-fan.html
The second Weightless Wonder (aka Vomit Comet) flight for the GYRE team in 2003 as part of the Reduced Gravity Student Flight Opportunities Program. Footage courtesy of NASA/JSC.
The first Weightless Wonder (aka Vomit Comet) flight for the GYRE team in 2003 as part of the Reduced Gravity Student Flight Opportunities Program. Footage courtesy of NASA/JSC.
The GYRE team's 2003 Test Equipment Data Package review in the Reduced Gravity Student Flight Opportunities Program. Footage courtesy of NASA/JSC.

Footage of the GYRE team's hypobaric chamber ride in 2003 as part of our training for our Weightless Wonder flight in the Reduced Gravity Student Flight Opportunities Program. Footage courtesy of NASA/JSC.
Quick demo of the hydraulic test platform I've been working on, under both manual and Arduino control

A quick test of the hydraulic positioning with closed-loop control using a very noisy flex sensor and a very primitive feedback algorithm. It works about as well as I expected, that is, hardly at all. But it's good to see the entire system working at all. Onwards and upwards.
Demo of the hydraulic test system now using the AS5040 rotary encoder chip and a (poorly tuned) real PID control loop.
The vanpool commute was more exciting than normal last week

videos.t: Prototype horizontal hip joint with hydraulic actuator
videos.desc: A quick demo of the horizontal hip joint being driven by the full-scale hydraulic actuator. The speed and power are somewhat terrifying.

A montage of very wet failures of the boat we built for the April Tools Wooden Boat Challenge in Madeira Park, BC. We only had 3 hours to build it, using only hand tools and a very limited set of materials. It was great fun, if not the most successful boat ever made. None of us had ever made one before, though, so we weren't too disappointed.

Demonstration of the hat I made to go with a friend's TARDIS dress project. It lights up and makes the VWORP VWORP sound at the push of a button. Inside is an Arduino and WaveShield.

For a more fanciful demonstration of the hat, see this video: http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LDoMO-kkVrQ

Full project page: http://www.attoparsec.com/artifacts/tardis.html

videos.t: Attoparsec 8 Channel EL Wire Interface Kit Demo
videos.desc:
Quick demonstration of the 8 channel EL wire interface kit that I'm selling through Attoparsec. I have it hooked to an Arduino which is running a simple binary output. This could also have been done with a 555 and a binary counter easily enough. While I assume most people using the kit will hook it to a microcontroller, it doesn't really care where the inputs come from. 

Why did I make it? Because the playa is filled with el wire all blinking at the same rate. We can do better than that! If you want to put together an impressive piece of el wire artwork, this kit is pretty much the easiest, c

videos.t: EL Wire Interface Kit Demo: Chaser
videos.desc: A simple demo of the Attoparsec EL Wire Interface Kit, showing a chaser effect. More information -- including the source code -- is available at: http://www.attoparsec.com/products/interface/

videos.t: EL Wire Interface Kit Demo: Fade In/Out
videos.desc: A simple demo of the Attoparsec EL Wire Interface Kit, showing a mass fade in/fade out effect. More information -- including the source code -- is available at: http://www.attoparsec.com/products/interface/

videos.t: EL Wire Interface Kit Demo: Binary Counter
videos.desc: A simple demo of the Attoparsec EL Wire Interface Kit, showing a binary counter effect. More information -- including the source code -- is available at: http://www.attoparsec.com/products/interface/

videos.t: EL Wire Interface Kit Demo: Cylon Chaser
videos.desc: A simple demo of the Attoparsec EL Wire Interface Kit, showing a Cylon chaser effect. More information -- including the source code -- is available at: http://www.attoparsec.com/products/interface/

videos.t: EL Wire Interface Kit Demo: Wave Chaser
videos.desc: A simple demo of the Attoparsec EL Wire Interface Kit, showing a fade in/fade out wave chaser effect. More information -- including the source code -- is available at: http://www.attoparsec.com/products/interface/

The first Kalamazoo update for 2011, showing the prototyped improved flywheel, new steering linkage, and steering lever lock mechanism. Looking to be on track for it to actually work at Burning Man this year.
A demonstration of the Kalamazoo without any flywheel, with the previous temporary flywheel, and with the new welded ring flywheel
Some video from the first Kalamazoo roadtest using the new and improved flywheel. It was very encouraging, with a much smoother action. The addition of passengers made it even better.
Quick roadtest to try out the new custom flywheel weights which I cast last week. They're conformal, branded, and much better looking. Whee!
A brief demonstration of Attoparsec's new Burning Man toy for 2011, the Skinner Box. Keep pedaling the bike and it randomly dispenses alcohol!
One of the videos from our scientific excursion and picnic kept converting at 2x speed. Once I saw the effect, I really couldn't resist doing the obvious.
After collecting all the footage from the Kalamazoo scientific expedition and picnic, I really had to put it all together as a music video for the most excellent Caravan Palace song Dragons. Enjoy!

Kº very graciously agreed to teach me some fire breathing at Burning Man 2011. This is the tail end of the lesson, including my best (still not very good) burst and then him taking a turn, showing how it's really done.

A demonstration of a new musical instrument invented by Attoparsec, the Hydrocrystallophone. (AKA the Glissando, AKA the Gliss, AKA the Mechanical Theramin.) It a mechanized glass harp, similar to Benjamin Franklin's glass armonica except capable of creating a range of tones using a single glass. It was first shown in public at Steamcon 2011.

I made a chainsword prototype for Halloween, but its performance was not what I had hoped. I've since rebuilt the guide bar to include a tip sprocket and switched to low profile saw chain. As you can see, it is now much more effective when defending against pumpkin threats. How it will serve against zombies has yet to be determined.

Next step will be to redo the handle to make it generally more sword-like in nature. Abslom Daak won't have anything on me!

People kept being late to the morning stand-ups at work. So I hacked a cheap pair of beacon lights to be battery powered and clamp on to the top of the whiteboard. Because what's the point of being scrum master if you don't use your rivet gun now and then?

This is a run of the harmonic pendulum system I created as a prototype for a much large art project for Burning Man 2012. The real focus was on the release mechanism, so the pendula themselves have high-friction pivots and don't swing for very long. Still it was a fun test!

videos.t: Harmonic Fire Pendula -- Improved Release Mechanism
videos.desc: A quick demo of the improved release mechanism on the 1/3 scale Harmonic Fire Pendula prototype.

An unlit demo of the improved Harmonic Fire Pendula prototype. It's not quite fully tuned yet, but it's getting pretty close and the mechanics are all done. There should be a video of it running at night with the kerosene torches attached soon.

videos.t: Harmonic Fire Pendula -- 1/3 Scale Prototype Night Test
videos.desc: A test of the HFP prototype at night, complete with flaming torches. With the mechanical design proven, all that is left to do is build the full-scale, 15 foot tall version!
An update of the progress on the Harmonic Fire Pendula, an honorarium project for Burning Man 2012.

videos.t: Harmonic Fire Pendula -- Final Construction Update
videos.desc:
One last quick update on the HFP status before everything gets packed up, showing the release mechanism linkage and the refueling bucket. Everything is go for a departure next week, getting onto the playa next Thursday. Look for the Harmonic Fire Pendula about 200 feet off Esplanade along the 6:45 radial.

As an experiment, this was entirely shot, edited and uploaded from my phone.
Brief clip of the full-scale HFP running on the playa the first night it was lit up.

videos.t: Harmonic Fire Pendula -- Deployment and Operation
videos.desc: The culmination of 8 months of work, this video shows the deployment and operation of the honorarium project Harmonic Fire Pendula at Burning Man 2012.
A couple weeks into a watch repair class, my first complete disassembly-cleaning-reassembly cycle is complete. Not too complicated, but I'm happy with the results.
Demo of the clockhat I made (but didn't quite finish in time) for Burning Man 2012. The clock face is set via servos and a laser-cut gear system.

A demonstration of the valve assembly prototype for the 2013 BarBot entry I'm working on, the Cocktail Engine. It uses a standard servo to open and close a valve via laser cut sprockets and bike chain.

A quick demonstration of the completed Cocktail Engine, Attoparsec's entry for the 2013 BarBot event. It uses a punch card interface to allow users to specify the ingredients they want in their drink.
A demo of the Jacquard mechanism at the Deutsch Technikmuseum Berlin.
A collection of shots of the Newcomen engine at the Black Country Living Museum, followed by a relevant piece of (slightly modified) poetry.
Some video of the Grand Junction 90 Inch Cornish Beam Engine at the Kew Bridge Steam Museum. Please excuse the weird vertical format, I was too distracted to think about how I was holding my camera.

A quick demo of the Google Glass enabled version of Sky Map I've been working on. It provides a simplified version of the options menu which can be accessed with a single tap. Layers can be turned on and off, as well as night mode. In addition, I've added a "Continents" layer which shows the outlines of landmasses as they would be seen if the Earth was transparent.

(Video captured with screencast over USB, which results in a very low framerate. The motion is smooth when run locally!)
A demonstration using the IR Blue wireless thermal camera module with Google Glass.

videos.t: Sprocket Welding -- Google Glass POV Test
videos.desc:
I wanted to test the process of recording shop work using Google Glass, so here is some work on the gimballed maze prototype.

Specifically, I'm curious if this can be useful even with minimal staging and editing. All of this was done in single takes, with only the most rudimentary of editing. I love the idea of sharing shop techniques through methods like this, but it has to be quick and easy to get the video made if I'm going to do it regularly.
Building and attaching the chain tensioners for the gimballed maze prototype. Shot through Google Glass, as part of my ongoing experiments in how to share shop work better.

An improved demonstration and explanation of the Cocktail Engine, a device made for the 2013 BarBot event. It is a robotic cocktail maker, electro-mechanical in nature and driven entirely by punchcards.

I put Glass on the head of the bounciest guitarist I know. This is the result.

WARNING MAY CAUSE MOTION SICKNESS

A fly through of the GMBLMZ initial design, Attoparsec's 2014 Burning Man project. It is a 4 meter gimbaled frame, allowing external control over each axis through cranks and chain drive. In the center is a 3D maze for a bowling ball. The trick, of course, will be in coordinating the motion of all 3 axes and keep the ball from falling off the tracks!
A quick demo of the GMBLMZ prototype and its inspiration. The full scale version is being built for Burning Man 2014.

videos.t: TRIKES for Unlimited Unofficial Unsanctioned Radical Self Liability 2014
videos.desc: The view forward and back from my death trike taking part in the 2014 TRIKES race down some very steep parts of Queen Anne hill in Seattle.
Picking up the first steel order for the GMBLMZ project
Demonstration of the layout jig for the cross braces on the GMBLMZ struts.
Short video of the GMBLMZ in action, at Burning Man 2014.

Attoparsec's installation GMBLMZ -- "a pilgrimage in three-space" -- at Burning Man 2014.

GMBLMZ is a 3D tube maze, inspired by kid's toys such as Perplexus. It is fully gimbaled inside a steel framework to allow rotation in any direction. The outer ring is 4 meters across, and the struts alone required over 6000 welds to build. It is operated using simple push-sticks, which keep participants more or less out of harm's way. Future revisions might include a crank and chain-drive system to allow more precise (and mechanically interesting!) control of each axis. External lighting was by 6 solar

videos.t: Mirror alignment process, Tim's Vermeer device
videos.desc: A quick demo of how to align the mirror when setting up a Tim's Vermeer device. This technique uses a second, non-mirrored copy of the original photograph to eliminate mirror skew.
I needed to make a quick kinetic sculpture for a local bike appreciation event. Tada!
Rendering of my proposal for the St. Helens Gateway Sculpture Project, Phase 2.
Installation kinetic/sonic sculpture for the City of Shoreline, built from an old piano, 12 sledge hammers, and a lot of steel. On display in August and September of 2015.
Short montage of the making of the 2015 Hugo Award bases.
Full walk-through of the process I used to make the 2015 Hugo Award bases.
Attoparsec's entry in the 2016 Cocktail Robotics Grand Challenge, a purely mechanical bar bot.
Rendering of the entire tesseract zoetrope design concept. Goal was to create an entirely mechanical 3D zoetrope using film projector techniques to eliminate the motion blur.

Rendering of the view through one of the viewing ports of the tesseract zoetrope design concept. Goal was to create an entirely mechanical 3D zoetrope using film projector techniques to eliminate the motion blur.

Rendering of the view through one of the viewing ports of the tesseract zoetrope design concept. Goal was to create an entirely mechanical 3D zoetrope using film projector techniques to eliminate the motion blur. Added a solid backdrop in this version to make the tesseract stand out better.

Rendering of the tesseract zoetrope design concept. Goal was to create an entirely mechanical 3D zoetrope using film projector techniques to eliminate the motion blur. Added a solid backdrop in this version to make the tesseract stand out better.

Time Machines is a kinetic sculpture installation sponsored by Spaceworks Tacoma. It consists of a pair of devices, each showing a matched "then-and-now" set of historical and modern photography of Tacoma. It was on display at 11th & Commerce in downtown Tacoma from January-March of 2017.
A quick and dirty demo of the Murmuration piece for VALA's Sculpture in Motion exhibit in Redmond, WA.

A flock of mechanical birds that circle when the crank is turned, inspired by 1980s artificial life experiments, specifically Craig Reynolds' simulation of bird flocks. Made for the “Sculptures in Motion” exhibit at VALA Eastside.

videos.t: Steam engine machining -- reversing mechanism bar
videos.desc: Time lapse of the machining done on the reversing mechanism bar for my Tiny Power "M" Center Crank engine.
Machining the reversing mechanism pivot for my Tiny Power "M" center crank engine.
Another build video of my Tiny Power "M" center crank steam engine project. This episode: the crankshaft bearing blocks!
The new carillon bells in the University of Washington's Red Square playing Ode to Joy as part of the dedication concert.
Testing my new inductive heater for doing the hot riveting work on the Tacoma Prairie Line Trail project. Very impressed with the speed and precision of how it heats!
Quick test of a smaller coil I made for the induction heater, sized for the 3/8" rivets the project is using.
What it was like to hammer in one out of the 346 rivets on the fake boiler for the Tacoma PLT project.
Been wanting to make something like this for awhile, whee!
Added ticking sounds, tweaked the animation a bit.
When touring Kentuck Knob, I was quite taken by the effect of walking under these apertures out on the deck.
Installation of the piece "Pressure" on the Prairie Line Trail in Tacoma, WA. (Between the Tacoma Art Museum and the Children's Museum.)

videos.t: Section of "Flow" on the Prairie Line Trail
videos.desc:
One section of text from "Flow", the companion piece to my sculpture "Pressure" on the Prairie Line Trail in downtown Tacoma.

Taken from a 1916 letter from Captain Matsuzo Sakamoto from Tacoma to his family in Yokohoma. His freighter, the Seiko Maru, sank with all hands on the voyage back.

Translation: "How are you and my family? Did you deliver a baby? Our vessel arrived at Victoria safely and has arrived Port Tacoma via Seattle at 12th March afternoon. We will leave Tacoma around 22nd. I’m supposed to arrive at Yokohama, Japan around 13th April."

A quick demo of Gottlob, the new programming language I've been developing. It is based on the gloriously idiosyncratic notation developed in Gottlob Frege's Begriffsschrift. The only logical operation is implication, which also doubles as a conditional. Universal quantifiers serve as for loops. In this example I build an equivalent to the following code:
for a in [1..2] 
   for b in [1..2] 
      var c = (a==1)  → ((b==1) → false))
      print(c)

In more conventional terms, c = (a==1) || (b==1). (Remember, implication returns true if the test fails! And in this notation, the test comes *afte

On the Infinite is a temporary installation at Dayton Street Plaza in Edmonds, WA. It is composed of three generations of a Hilbert curve, which was one of the first fractals to be discovered and/or invented. As the iterations proceed towards infinity, the curve begins to transcend its one-dimensional origin.

videos.t: One hour at Yarrow Point Freeway Station
videos.desc: I recently collected 55 minutes of video showing the predicted arrival time of buses as displayed on a reader board along with the actual arrivals, in order to test a hypothesis. This is what it looked like at 60x realtime.

Between July 14 and July 24, 2019, the @ApolloLego project reenacted the Apollo 11 mission on Twitter. Every image was posted 50 years to the minute after the original event it depicts.

Obviously, the only thing to do after that was to spend a week writing a script that would take the original planning spreadsheet and automagically turn it into a full movie, complete with a continuous mission timer! (...and then spend another few weeks tweaking everything so the work spent on writing the script was almost certainly pointless. But fun!)

I needed a cylindrical cam for a mechanism in a kinetic sculpture that I'm prototyping. Making it was a fun, if lengthy, process.

videos.t: Manhattan Project plutonium box replica build
videos.desc:
For Halloween 2019 I wanted a replica of the carrying case used for the plutonium cores in the Manhattan Project. This is how I went about making it.

The Restricted Data post that first got me obsessed: http://blog.nuclearsecrecy.com/2011/11/25/friday-image-posing-with-the-plutonium/

Most of the historical photography is from Los Alamos National Laboratory's Flickr account: https://www.flickr.com/photos/losalamosnatlab/

Getting back to working on the Clapping Machine prototype, this time making a replacement for the tragically useless cylindrical cam shown in a previous video: https://youtu.be/QOvj0OjmTzk

Lessons learned: I start sections by saying "okay" way too much. And I devoice "curve" to the point where it sounds more like "kerf", which I never realized before.

My replica of the Manhattan Project plutonium box will be joining the collection at the Bradbury Science Museum in Los Alamos! That meant I had to fix the hideous knurling on the handle assembly thumb screws.


See my previous video for more information on this project: https://youtu.be/RFHQdXxLj8M
I got an old mining lamp and explored its operation.
Since I'm trying to make videos more frequently, I thought it would be a good idea to improve my camera mounts a bit.

videos.desc:
I've started work on a storefront installation due next month, featuring 111 chaotically spinning fidget spinners.


Original inspiration: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-z3SG5RvWbY

Continuing work on my new kinetic sculpture A Study in Chaos. This week I get all the spinners drilled for the magnets and get started making the motor coupling for the driven spinners.


Good news: audio quality will be improving soon as I now have a proper wireless lav mic.

videos.t: A Study in Chaos #3: Mounts, frames and stands
videos.desc: I finish the motor mounts, weld up the frames and get started on the stands for my upcoming kinetic installation A Study in Chaos. Now with somewhat better audio quality!

videos.desc: This wraps up the construction of A Study in Chaos, including what is hopefully the resolution of a bad last-minute problem with how the spinners were operating.
Installation of the completed piece.

videos.t: Pneumatic Slide Whistle #1: Experimentation and slide mechanism
videos.desc: Starting a new project, inspired by the Hazard Fraught coupon sheet that comes across my feed every few years.
I recently got a chance to visit the Panama Canal. It seemed a shame not to share it, so a new "On Assignment" video series has been born.
Getting back to the pneumatic slide whistle project, this week making a nozzle prototype with surprisingly good results.

videos.t: Pneumatic Slide Whistle #3: Finalizing the aperture
videos.desc: The actual whistle pipe gets its aperture cut and the air-shaping baffle inserted.

videos.t: Pneumatic Slide Whistle #4: Air connection adapter
videos.desc: Making a proper air connection for the main whistle pipe. First time doing a second video in the same week, as a way to keep busy and not think about The Event.
Trying to do my part for the emergency mask sewing efforts, I explore the possibility of using a die to cut fabric patterns with mixed results.

videos.t: Pneumatic Slide Whistle #5: Rethinking the baffle
videos.desc: Experimentation with a ramped baffle to reduce the weediness of the sound of the slide whistle.

videos.t: Horological Trigon: Sundials, geometry, and the The Art of Dialling
videos.desc: I took a deep dive into how the geometric constructions used to design sundials work, and ended up replicating a 17th century scientific instrument in the process.

videos.t: Helping with Faceshield Production (And what gauge blocks tells us about inductive reasoning)
videos.desc:
While working to help a local faceshield effort, I stumbled into a lengthy tangent exploring an unexpected connection between gauge blocks and the philosophy of science.


Will Gauge Blocks Stick In Vacuum?: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jNEvS_bjKIo

videos.t: Pneumatic Slide Whistle #6: Finishing the sloped baffle
videos.desc: Quick little update this week, wherein I finish the sloped baffle to channel the air more smoothly into the whistle aperture.

I return to the Horological Trigon to finish it all proper with dial wax and silvering powder.


Previous work on this project: https://youtu.be/RUySYTK7yDk

This was my talk for !!Con 2020, filmed ahead of time due to social distancing. It covers the background of my esoteric programming language Gottlob, and explores some of the lessons I learned from it about how the notation of logical operators developed over the centuries.

I have recently been getting into the modular synth world, starting by building a lot of kits to keep costs down. To keep costs down even further, I decided to try making a clock modular from scratch.



(Sorry for the lower video quality, a recent Adobe update has completely broken my export capabilities.)

videos.desc: Since I've been doing a lot more electronics recently, I decided to upgrade my soldering tools. In this video I made a replacement shell for the iron tip cleaning wool.

My patch cables were already getting out of control, so I grabbed some scrap metal and went out to the mill.

This was one of the first custom module ideas I had when I first started obsessing over modular: use an old rotary phone dial as a pulse generator! The new case had room for it, so I made one. It's not, maybe, the MOST useful module ever. But that's okay.

I saw some modules with music boxes attached, but none of them were motorized, much less with CV speed control. So I decided I had to make one. 

Demo of the final system starts at: 5:09

The chain drive I used is 1/8" pitch plastic from SDP-SI. I previously used it in my kinetic sculpture Murmuration: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UcVa08qiZvM
